items.body:
Hamburg’s post-punk goth wraiths play the hits for John Peel, slinging cuts sifted from their four sessions recorded 1982-1985, including tearing renditions of ‘Incubus Succubus’ and ‘Qual’, a thunderous ‘Sehnsucht’, the very Cocteaus-esque ‘Polarlicht’, and tortured romance of ‘Autumn’

"You only need listen to the soul-devouring nocturnal visitation of Incubus Succubus, or the obliterating fury of Qual (“Meine Wiege ist deine Grab” – “my cradle is your grave”) to see that underestimating Xmal Deutschland was never a good idea. When the Hamburg band first walked into the BBC’s Maida Vale Studio in November 1982 to record their debut session for John Peel, it was natural they should feel a flash of awe as they were ushered through the labyrinthine building, on the brink of joining a radio lineage that included The Fall, David Bowie, Siouxsie And The Banshees and The Cure. Yet the band – at that point singer Anja Huwe, keyboardist Fiona Sangster, guitarist Manuela Rickers, drummer Manuela Zwingmann and bassist Wolfgang Ellerbrock – also quickly picked up on the old-school energy and hierarchies of the place, the entrenched divisions between tea ladies and the producers and sound engineers, the tensions between the old-school male rock’n’roll way of doing things and their band’s place in the modern world.

John Peel rarely came to the studio to meet the bands he had selected for the honour of a Peel Session, having no interest in pressing the showbiz flesh (For Lulu or otherwise). Instead, as Sangster recalls, Xmal Deutschland immediately found themselves up against producers and engineers who, regardless of the blessing inherent in Peel’s invitation, weren’t terribly impressed with the sight of this female-majority German band. “They communicated quite clearly that they didn’t think you were very good, that they didn’t like the music, and would you please hurry up,” says Sangster, bristling at the memory 43 years later.

Yet Xmal Deutschland had – in the jaded language of the old-fashioned male-dominated music industry – very much paid their dues by the time they arrived at Maida Vale. They formed in Hamburg in 1980 – “a tough city,” says singer Anja Huwe, a significantly grittier place than the artier musical enclaves of Cologne or Dusseldorf. They had endured – and thrived – in their canal-side rehearsal studio, against all the health-and-safety odds. The punks next-door had soundproofed their space with egg boxes; when somebody dropped a cigarette, the solvent went up in flames. “All dirty carpets and grotty sofas,” recalls Sangster. “It was filthy, it was damp, it was cold.” Zwingmann, meanwhile, recalls the dangerous swerving of their VW van as they raced for late-night ferries, burdened with equipment.

They had shown their own grit, too, by making the decision early on that they were not going to be channelled into the Neue Deutsche Welle, then a buzzword for young German bands. “If we’d stayed in Hamburg and gone down that path, our career would have been over in a year,” explains Huwe. “Because it was a very short-lived movement.” After releasing their first two singles on Hamburg imprint ZickZack, in 1983 they found the label that could match their questing, independent energy. “We recorded a tape in the rehearsal room and we took it to 4AD,” recalls Sangster. “We didn’t go anywhere else.” Fetish, their debut album for the label, followed. Like formidable, backcombed Groucho Marxes, they never wanted to belong to any club that would want them as a member. “We just didn’t want to give them the obvious sort of thing, and we always kept our distance from everyone,” says Huwe. “We were like a group on our own. We never went to a place like the Batcave – and they always invited us. Everyone wanted us to join, but we never went there because we were not interested. We went to exhibitions, we wrote books, saw films – you know, enjoyed our own company.”

This record, a fabulous chronological document of the four Peel sessions they recorded between November 1982 (five months before the release of their 1983 debut album Fetisch) and May 1985, is the sound of a band who knew the power of that company and who ultimately refused to be intimidated by the gruffly condescending gatekeepers of Maida Vale. They found a strength in defying their old-school attitudes. “We benefited from that because we sort of got into ‘fuck you’ mode”, says Sangster, much to Huwe and Zwingmann’s delight. “That might be part of the energy that you’re hearing.”

It’s an energy that transmits with a piercing clarity in these sixteen tracks, the constraints of time and space giving what Sangster calls “a certain urgency” to these sessions. “Listening back, you can tell it’s sort of like a hybrid between a live performance and a studio performance,” she says. “These are different versions, which is what makes them interesting.”

As Huwe and Sangster stress, a Peel session wasn’t the time for Xmal Deutschland to experiment – “you would choose one of the bangers!” they laugh. That’s clear from the opening full-pelt Incubus Succubus, its supernatural vortex immediately transporting the listener right into the room, to the dreamy expanses of closing track Autumn (from May 1985), their first song in English. In between arcs the remarkable career of a band in constant motion: “It’s a really interesting snapshot, as it were, of our evolution, these four Peel Sessions all together,” says Sangster. “You can see how we grew as a band.” It’s there in untethered experimentalism and proto-Mandinka howls of Reigen, from their second album Tocsin, or the new expansiveness that comes with Nachtschatten’s twinkling synths (not a million miles away from The Cure’s pop experiments) or the gorgeous melody of Der Wind. Here are the fierce hexes of their early work – the angel-devil showdown of Geheimnis, Qual’s scything B-side Sehnsucht, the tribal skitter of In Motion – mutating into a different kind of spellbinding. The studio atmosphere might have been oppressive, but this collection of Peel Sessions shows a band making the space their own. “It was so different compared to how we lived, because it was British, very conservative,” says Huwe. “But we jumped in there.” With this compilation, you can hear the ripples Xmal Deutschland made then still powerfully resonating down the years."

items.body:
The jittery pulses and waking dream-like atmospheres of Dx2ov land on London’s Blank Mind for an album strafing between cut-up sound poetry and whisked garage-house.

“Dx2ov arrives on Blank Mind with Tonegues, his second vinyl LP following on from Interzona on Gost Zvuk in 2024. The LP title is a wordplay on the idea of speaking in tongues and sonic tonalities, echoing the process and dialogue that went into creating the record. Taken from a vast archive of material from 2019-2025, these ideas were arranged with the collaboration of label owner Sam Purcell and then completed with the long-distance assistance of Toupaz.

Tonegues is best seen through the lens of a beat-tape, with the playful flow and variety that the format provides, bursting with oddball ideas and punctuated with intangible vocal samples. Much like the LP’s beguiling, hand-drawn artwork by Wolfgang Matuschek, it is a glimpse into an inner world, a portal to somewhere uncanny and strange borne through imagination.

Light dub flourishes mix with footwork/IDM hybrids and understated, melancholic synthesis on ‘2018’, whilst the loose, rhythmic march of ‘Fon32’ evokes the dusty beatdown styles of early 2000s Detroit downtempo records. Whilst on one of the LP highlights ‘Trout’ he lays down a gleefully strange bed for the surrealist storytelling of Jacob Dwyer about interactions with dogs, dripping old houses and a perennial wish for the phone to ring with a heavy dub poetry slant. Dx2ov swiftly moves through more footwork adjacent, almost bedroom hyper-pop territories with a penchant for gabber kicks on ‘No Strings (feat DJ Paprika)’ and the maximalism of album closer 'Demetch' which continues in the tradition of wonky, mid-2010s UK bass music flips. The outcome is a confounding, unorthodox piece of work, zigzagging between forms, textures and moods.”

items.body:
Produced by Neek and Jabu's Amos Childs (aka O$VMV$M), Manonmars' third album is syrupy suite of smoke-hazed recollections and free associated reflections set to decelerated, semi-rhythmic bumps, sluggish samples and cloudy drones. Sturdy biz FFO Ka, MIKE, King Vision Ultra or Coby Sey.

Manonmars' 2018 debut is one of those albums we still go back to periodically. It's that rare meeting of minds: a space for O$VMV$M to flex their production muscle and a scratchpad for London-based MC, painter and photographer Jack Martyn Richardson to sketch out his vision of England. And his experiences and impressions on 'Entertainment System' still feel chewable. "Goddess on my arm and both our phones got no service," he quips on 'Goddess'. "Acid is lysergic, psychedelic rock is Turkish." His rhymes aren't throwaway, they map out an underground that's very recognisable, shadowed by O$VMV$M's tuff, effective soundscapes - beats that reference trip-hop, ambient music, exotica and '70s movie soundtracks as much as they do US rap. On opener 'Flam3throw3r', Mars raps in double-time over shrill horns that blot out any trace of a beat; Neek and Childs sound as if they're relishing the negative space, adding chic sword swipes to a track that's got little else to do with the Wu Tang Clan. And even when a lumbering beat kicks in on 'Decathlon', flipping from downtempo to no-tempo in the final act, it sounds as if it's just there to assert O$VMV$M's commitment to slowness - Mars doesn't even seem to notice, rhyming casually but never losing his internal flow.

On 'Nasyua', his slurred expressions duck and weave around industrial whirrs and animalistic groans. "There was a time when I had flaws now I've adapted," he slurs. "I hit the zoot like Steve Zissou in 'The Life Aquatic' / then I dashed it, Christian Bale in a facemask on some Bat shit." Bristol mainstays Franco Franco and Dali de Saint Paul turn up to assist on 'Volcanic Shield', one of the album's most conventional bangers, led by O$VMV$M's skittering Surf Gang-like beats and morse code blips, and cold light's Birthmark lends his voice to 'Infinite', going bar for bar with Mars over Neek and Childs' soupy slackened funk. These moments are when 'Entertainment System' really shines, blaring out like an old tape on a busted in-car audio system. 'Firewater' takes the same approach, leaving Mars to do his best as snares are reformed into splashes alongside sultry stabs and sax from Brum-based sound artist Lorenzo Prati. "My bitch white, she can scuba dive and ice climb," he spits. "Put the drink down, I wasn't in my right mind." It's music that laughs through the tears - what could be more British than that?

items.body:
Absolutely filthy/screwed club gunk  and no-wave machine music from Murray Collier (Grim Lusk, Dip Friso) & Conal Blake (Feedback Moves, Domestic Exile), working together as Inweys and highly tipped FFO Actress, MMM, Wino, V/Vm's 'Machine Component' series...

“Inweys debut release arrives as four pieces of broken body music. Lurking, barely human fragments brought into the present. Using a short drum-machine improvisation as core material, the pieces are formed from a processes of mining and re-mining for small details, with each fragment zoomed in on and turned into new pieces. There’s a transformation taking place, but one that doesn’t obscure the materiality of the recording tapes as sticky, corrosive matter. On skewed and stretched fabric they enact their palimpsestic play, sketching and altering the grid with itchy technologies. What their edits and improvisations don’t say they let space say the rest, with vacuum aerated frames for bass to diffuse and beats to wriggle. More King Tubby than Cage, more Mantronix than Reich: minimalism with molten tips.

Both Conal and Murray’s past work has embraced malleable and iterative technologies; music whose feeliness figures itself out in space in a messy precomposed/improvised dialectic. This is the sort of thing most “new music” experimentalists (or anyone who spends most of their time obsessively manipulating tapes in expensive studios) often can’t achieve; a liveness, birthed from learning in situated play. Like the lore of Phuture’s Acid Trax, a poverty of material is at the heart of this, rendering the work with an abortive conviction: a corpse waking to consciousness becomes amphibious. Instead of the composer we have a relation, two people navigating the awkward spooling between the two reels of tape. Inweys is scots for “inwards”, and in their working process this is what they do. But the result is circular motion. Until the tape runs out, all in ways move out”. "

Fielding Hope.

items.body:
London-based Malaysian-Australian composer and professor Silvia Lim prioritises close listening on 'Flare', writing quiet, minimal patterns that draw attention to unusual textures and bewitching dissonances.

Having bounced between Malaysia, Australia and the UK growing up, Lim is fascinated by the idea of instability and how that might be represented sonically. She explores a certain kind of fragility on 'Flare', working with the flimsiness of timbre by zooming in to capture the most incidental sounds - the scraping of a slowly pulled bow on the strings or the softness of air blown through a bass clarinet's reed. On the two-part composition 'Grafting', Lim folds in unexpectedly beautiful melodies, letting them grind to a halt completely, or disappear into faint traces beneath resonant ghost notes and stifled wails. There's a trace of folk music in there, buried in the undergrowth. 

And on the four-part 'Field of Play', Lim prepares her instruments with a single tool each time: a hair clip, a bobby pin and piece of cork, presenting the pieces as proof of what sonic shifts these seemingly light preparations might cause. On 'contact', the bobby pin disintegrates the instrumentation, turning the strings into lightly boiling, echoing resonances and on 'hidden place', it's even more disorienting, sounding as if the cello is being lowered slowly into a vast metallic chamber.

items.body:
Alex Zhang Hungtai pivots yet again on 'Orion/Mother', playing (mostly) trumpet alongside some of the New York City underground scene's most intriguing improvisers, including Kwami Winfield, Laura Cocks, Lester St. Louis, TAK Ensemble's Madison Greenstone, 75 Dollar Bill's Che Chen and Leo Chang.

 'Orion/Mother' has its roots in a set of home recordings Zhang made with some of his talented local friends; "playing with you all deeply informed my current understanding in improvisation," he explains in his thank you note, "without you this album would not have existed." So over a two week period, in a rehearsal space in New York, he invited a handful of his friends to start "an ad-hoc group", playing trumpet over chopped up home recordings and wrenching them into the future. And while the finished article - split into two distinct sections - is long, it's fully worthy of your attention. As always, Zhang brings a unique ear into the room, resisting any usual improv tropes to concentrate on sounds that most artists would avoid - unruly resonances, glitches, off-piste rhythms and unsubtle interferences.

At it's best, the record sounds like jazz specters vanishing thru faded noise remnants and the wreckage of lost experiments. On 'Shadow Integration', Zhang's brassy wails echo out over a slippery, semi-rhythmic drum machine pattern, and on 'Tanhäuser Gate', the trumpet is even more isolated, weeping over a muted soundscape that's credited simply as "Ableton" on the accompanying notes. He maintains the same energy when he's working side-by-side with his collaborators, too, finding space for Winfield's circuit bent belches on 'Nataraja' and Chen and Chang's percussion on the jaw-droppingly spannered opener 'Sidewinder'. And even when the tone shifts on 'Mother', heading into a lighter (comparatively at least) zone on the woodwind-heavy 'Kali', Zhang has a knack for tying everything together with his lyrical performance. Just peep the title track, almost seven minutes of uncanny clanks and Tōru Takemitsu-strength murmurs that Zhang butters with pure improvised emotion.

London/Helsinki label Cold Blow map the subliminal links of early ‘90s electro, techno and its backroom, downbeat offshoots thru a plethora of tunes recorded ’92-’99 by the likes of Stasis, 2000 And One, CiM, all displaying how they translated Detroit techno intricacies and new age ambient soul for UK & EU bodies in motion, or those eaten by sofas.

“Across eight carefully selected slices of starry-eyed machine soul, Cold Blow presents an exquisite tour through backroom techno and downtempo electro. With a focus on thematic flow and an immersive listening experience, the London-based label explores works from leading lights of the 1990s and previously unreleased cuts that celebrate the human heart that can be discovered in synthetic sound practices.

The development of techno in the 1990s saw the music evolve in different directions across the world. From the expressive blueprint laid out by the Detroit pioneers, a wide range of tempos and energies emerged. Techno's evocative synthesis and intricate drum machine programming was especially potent for deeper explorations away from the dancefloor.

Documents Of Different Reality casts back to when technology was steering quantum leaps in communication and creativity and the future was shot through with naive optimism. It was also a time when the media and industry hadn't caught up with the music to box it into distinct categories. As such, there's a sense of creative freedom that informs the older tracks on the album, from 2000 And One and Sandy Huner's (originally as Pure) sparkling example of early Dutch techno to London-based LA Synthesis' detailed take on braindance and the majestic night sky vision of cult legend Stasis.

There's also space for rare, late 90s machine funk from Icelandic outlier Thor alongside Connective Zone's charmingly fractured bleep dream and a more contemporary offering from Barcelona-based duo Permutation. Meanwhile Mind Control and CiM both capture the spirit of stylistic fusion with twitchier rhythms that take influence from hardcore and jungle as much as techno.

With an atmospheric through-line of melancholic pads and harmonious leads, this small but perfectly formed collection naturally follows on from previous, equally thought-out compilations on Cold Blow, and adds a distinct perspective on the history and continuing legacy of pioneering early ambient techno.”

items.body:
Playing the kacapi, a Sundanese box zither, XKatedral alumnus Svennson leads a trio with violinist Maya Bennardo and bass clarinet player Erik Blennow Caläv on 'For a Lemon Tree', meditating on pitch and negative space.

Made up of two long pieces, the album highlights not just Svennson's writing, but the trio's interplay. The initial, title track is a fully notated piece that emerged from their improvisations; it's reined in, in many ways, condensed but still featuring the tonal experimentation that defines their experimentation. Working in 11-limit Just Intonation tuning, the trio work in tiny gestures - Svennson's kacapi plucks are most evident at the beginning, but the sounds that croak from Caläv's clarinet and Bennardo's violin are just as beguiling.

And as impressive as that short-form track is, the lengthy 'Improvisation on Prakāśa' takes it to another level. As the title suggests, this one's fully improvised and illustrates the relationship the players have with each other. It's chilling stuff that doesn't reveal itself straight away; Svennson's kacapi sounds almost medieval at times, while Bennardo creates toneless, whooshing textures that transport us to another dimension entirely.

DJ Plead and rRoxymore with a sick debut collab of rhythmelodically restless productions, infusing limber, freewheeling styles with subtly psychedelic balearic melodics - a big one for followers of CCL, Batu, Nick León, Olof Dreijer, Joe, Nídia & Valentina Magaletti.

After meeting for the first time in 2019, Hermione Frank and Jarred Beeler got together at Frank's Berlin studio, slowly sculpting fractal geometries before finally adding the finishing spit and polish at Beeler's parents’ house in Sydney. Marking some of the first original material from either in a minute, the EP knits the duo’s rhythmic fascinations in three ways. 

‘Celestial’ splices a rolling 4/4 with quicksilver polyrhythms and zippy melodic motifs swept into hand-clap trills, imagining something like Olof Dreijer re-shaping Joe’s angular syncopations. ‘Read Wrong’ follows to foreground a thumb piano on a more pendulous, sub-weighted flex, inflected with DJ Plead’s signature palette of drum sounds and canny orchestral flashes at the right moments, dipping like D1’s more melodic works or that forthcoming Nídia & Valentina Magaletti pearl. 

The duo save their most hard-hitting for last, sliding speedy, dembow-inspired geometries through green-tinted clouds of electronics on a UKF-compatible offbeat threaded with swooping subs and flighty flutes. The momentum never lets up, but the two producers manage to evoke a mood that's as suited to a late-nite solo thing as it is to peak time wreckage. In other words; deceptively effortless gear that hits harder the louder it gets.

Inspired by Ennio Morricone, J.J. Cale and Hindustani classical music, Michael Brook's 1992 4AD debut is a 2nd wave ambient/new age classic, finally remastered and bundled with the genius follow-up EP 'Live at the Aquarium'. Unmissable FFO Jon Hassell, Harold Budd, Daniel Lanois, Brian Eno and David Sylvian.

Brook is best known for his soundtrack work at this point - his influential scores for films like 'An Inconvenient Truth' and 'The Fighter' - but rewind back to the early 1990s and he was living in London, jobbing as a producer and working with Brian Eno. He'd released a few records by that point, collaborating with Eno and Daniel Lanois on his Editions EG debut 'Hybrid' and collaborating with Dutch artist Pieter Nooten on the excellent 'Sleeps with the Fishes' in 1987. But his most important contribution had arguably been his Infinite Guitar, a modified electric guitar that allowed him to play long sitar-like drones. He used that technique on Jon Hassell's beloved 1986 album 'Power Spot' and famously built an instrument for the Edge, who played it on 'With or Without You'. And while he was working with other musicians, he was sketching out ideas for this next record, working slowly in his bedsit in-between commercial work and attempting to adapt the music he loved, particularly bluegrass and the work of Indian flute player Pannalal Ghosh.

Unsurprisingly, it's Brook's guitar sounds that take the lead from the beginning, muddled with woozy synths and assistance from a team of his close associates: Brian Eno, Daniel Lanois, Roger Eno, Dead Can Dance's James Pinker, violinist Hahn Rowe, Hassell collaborator Richard Henderson and viola player Nell Catchpole. The music is very much of its era, a core text for 4AD or Les Disques Du Crepusule heads, and illustrates just how quickly "ambient" and "new age" music were evolving. Brook hadn't been classically trained, so was urged by Hassell to do some lessons with La Monte Young, an experience that had led him to the Infinite Guitar in the first place. But long sustain wasn't the beginning and end of his interest in Hindustani classical music or in 20th century minimalism. You can hear just how the genres were being re-codified here, how traditional rhythms were being re-interpreted on drum machines and how Steve Reich's and Philip Glass's innovations were being absorbed by wide-eyed onlooker long before they became rave's after-hours staples.

If the album sounds a little frilly 35 years after its original release, that's mostly because Brook's sound was jumped on by Hollywood remarkably quickly. Just three years after 'Cobalt Blue' was released, the track 'Ultramarine' was conspicuously placed in Michael Mann's 'Heat' alongside selections from Terje Rydpal, Lisa Gerrard and Brian Eno. And he quickly became a staple, contributing to Hans Zimmer soundtracks like 'Mission: Impossible 2' and 'Black Hawk Down' and working on prestige projects like 'Into the Wild' and 'Brooklyn'. So if you're interested in hearing a more stripped down version of the album, then 4AD handily bundled it with 'Live at the Aquarium ' when they reissued the album for the first time in 1999. The show was recorded at the press party for the release of 'Cobalt Blue' and features Brook on his own, playing even more passionately and demonstrating the nuance of his signature technique.

Softly softly does it for the gorgeous debut duo of soundtrack composer Elori Saxl & saxophonist Henry Solomon with their lushly ephemeral grasp of 4th world ambient jazz, tipped for the anyone on the line between Lynch/Badalamenti, TLF Trio, Laurel Halo, Arve Henriksen or Alex Zhang-Hungtai's Love Theme side-wind.

Captured over a few days in LA, ‘Seeing Is Believing’ frames the sax player’s searching feel for tone across soundscapes sparingly coloured in subtle harmonic gradients by Elori Saxl’s fluttering Juno 106 keys. The nine parts are testament to the duo’s near-telepathic level of intuition and mutual vision of a palpably tissue-soft atmospheric music; one where spectres of ’70s minimalism and ’80s new age bleed forward into structures equally informed by soundsystem culture and contemporary pop production, achieving a sort of slow shifting, ecological pressure system that is a pleasure to sink into.

Within her richly visual, implicitly storytelling style, Elori Saxl draws on a wellspring of experience in composing for new music ensembles, and soundtracking and directing films for New Yorker and Slate, to set spacious dimensions for Solomon’s ruminative baritone sax and bass clarinet to wander freely. A quiet sense of restraint defines proceedings as their forms gently grow and sway from the dusky licks of ‘Reverence’ thru the gauzy lustre of the title piece, conjuring a geosmin waft in ‘Raindrops’ and LA hills panorama on ‘Reno Silver’, or balmiest breeze of Glass-like phrasing on ‘A Thousand Steps’, into the gorgeous, pitch bent and sensual sorcery summoned in standout ‘Heart.’

Stunner.

New LP from NY rapper Chuck Strangers aka Che Jessamy.

"Chuck Strangers's latest, Glory Of The King's Hand, represents a matured, self-assured attitude and an emphasis on songcraft. “I made a lot of conscious [musical] decisions," says the heavy-tongued griot from East Flatbush, Brooklyn. “I really tried to make better songs that people might want to hear again.” To accomplish this, Chuck chose to be a producer in the Quincy Jones sense, bringing together vocalists, producers, and musicians. The results are astounding. Take for instance, “Breaking Atoms,” a track built on the improvisations of production trio/band Human Error Club. A hypnotic Fender-Rhodes and headnod-inducing drums perfectly complement Chuck and billy woods’ vivid verses followed by Zeroh’s psychedelic vocals.

The list of contributing producers is a who’s who of sound scientists including The Alchemist, Animoss, Theravada, Kenny Segal, Preservation, and Child Actor. And while Glory … is a cross-section of the underground in 2026, what Chuck brings to the table is uniquely Chuck Strangers."

items.body:
The inimitable DeForrest Brown, Jr. caps off his Speaker Music project with a final set of expressionistic technoid evolutions, editing live improvisations into studio-corrupted projections of his musical mind map that runs through jazz, trap, shoegaze, dub and drone. Essential listening whether you're into Miles, Drexciya or Autechre.

Primarily used to mean a "summary" of sorts, the word synoptic is often found in connection with Biblical scholarship, grouping the New Testament gospels of Matthew, Mark and Luke together because of their similarities. And on 'Speaker Music', Brown attempts to isolate comparable harmonies between various Black musical strands, examining the marching band music he grew up playing, Sun Ra and experimental jazz, and realising how all this factors into the development of electronic music, steering its course even now. Brown calls the project "theory first", an analysis of rhythm in Black music as it pertains to his landmark text 'Assembling a Black Counter Culture'. And it's run its course at this stage; if you've heard 2023's excellent 'Techxodus' or its predecessors, you'll already know the general theme - a sonic space where free jazz, footwork, gospel and noise exists at once in spiritual harmony.

Brown's final act as Speaker Music is to take recordings from his residencies at Troy's EMPAC and Vancouver's Libby Leshgold Gallery and sculpt them into dense "studio-as-instrument" snapshots of his theory. He starts with Don Lewis, the musician and engineer (and nuclear weapons specialist) who developed a pre-MIDI sound controller for analog synthesizers that he called the LEO, or Live Electronic Orchestra. Brown uses this methodology to guide his own setup (on iPad, MacBook and mixer), using software modules, effects units and drum machines to simulate Lewis's arsenal of vintage boxes, then transports the results to the studio for "post production editing, overdubbing and spacial manipulation." He ends up with a sound that's constantly changing, on the one hand driven by the skittering techno-to-trap drum sequences that powered his other records and on the other zeroing in on the sonic density and physicality of set texts like A Guy Called Gerald's 'Black Secret Technology' and Miles Davis's ornery and prophetic masterpiece 'On The Corner'.

On opener 'Techno-Vernacular Expressionism', Brown makes the direction clear by ducking the whirring hi-hats and syncopated kicks deep beneath elasticated and saturated dub-echoed chords. Even when the rhythms are moved closer to the spotlight on 'Saecularhythmia...' they're muddled with remnants of those same chords, spliced alongside Brown's own decelerated half-human monologs. These experiments open the floodgates for a sequence of punk-ier experiments that consider the impact of sound on the body itself, taking into account not just rhythm but tone, timbre and distortion. On 'Chaosmosis', Brown's obsessively edited beat sequences are set, 'Amber'-like, against a single growling synth note and on the title track, he uses rhythmelodic hits and coarse feedback to herald a psych-jazz pivot into oscillatory mayhem in the third act. It's a record that constantly collapses and rebuilds itself, turning Drexciyan electro sequences into chiming church bells on the brilliant 'GLO//A' and day zero techno into euphoric nu-gaze on  the crushing finale, 'Dhalgren (Nihilism is Not Enough)'. We're gonna miss Speaker Music, but we've got a feeling this isn't the last we'll hear from Brown.

Rising Maryland rapper Zel teams with Surf Gang regular FLEA DIAMONDS on 'I.T.R.', adding his slurred, hazy recollections to the producer's brief and brittle beats.

Zel reached notoriety only a few months back, releasing his weighty 'Still Right Here' mixtape and standardizing the gravelly wyrd-rap sound he's been plugging away at for some time now, working routinely with fellow outsider Xang under the DPM tag. Here, his appetite for the obscure is still voracious; FLEA DIAMONDS digs through his archive for his murkiest cues, cutting washy field recordings with boxy toms and busted synths on 'Trailblazin/Loaded' while Zel stumbles precariously over the bare bones of a beat. And 'Scripts/Open Season' is even less straightforward, drifting from early coherence into a blackened crisp of fingersnaps and subs that Zel graces with his chewed-up rhymes.

The only breather comes from Surf Gang figurehead evilgiane, who skews the batshit 'Aint Shit Funny' with fuzzed-out ambient loops that sounds as if they've been snatched from Akira Yamaoka's 'Silent Hill' OST.

items.body:
Hi-energy electronic dance music from Northern Ghana via Studio Simpa. Compilation showcasing Dickson Gawani, Bala Zaaku, Yaa Naara and others.

"Relentless percussion, trance loops, heavy autotune and slinky VST synths. Sourced from locally-released VCDs circulating the markets of Dagbon and entirely unavailable outside the region until now.

Studio Simpa collects tracks from the past decade of the neo-traditional Dagbani dance genre - a modernized version of the traditional percussion dance - produced by Mohamed “Ebony” Fuseini, a self taught producer, recording drums on his phone and recreating the sound of traditional music via FL Studio. Collaborating with “Gawani” – flashy singers from the surrounding villages - and local VCD producers, Ebony recorded new hyper-electronic versions of simpa for the burgeoning local video market, complete with suggestive videos of women shaking their hips - light cultural transgression in the predominantly Muslim Dagbani North.

The compilation showcases the top artists of the scene - Dickson Gawani, Bala Zaaku, Yaa Naara and others - across a range of style and subject, from political commentary to warrior clan rhythms. Includes extensive liner notes by Morgan Greenstreet with artist interviews, cultural history, and song translations. Debut release on the Sahel Sounds imprint Autotune the World."

Cult Polish producer Przemysław Jankowiak, aka 2K88, assembles a choice team of UK collaborators on 'Everything Always Changes', visualizing a "hypnagogic R&B" symphony that flickers, fades and fully folds in on itself, transforming its raw elements into poetic fragments and half-heard hooks. Magickal biz, honestly - RIYL Kelela, Space Afrika, Malibu, Yungwebster, Romance.

We know, we use the word "cinematic" is just plain nah, but occasionally it's kinda necessary - 2K88's music just cycles at 24 frames per second seemingly all on its own, lubricated by his hand-picked coconspirators: Preston's Rainy Miller, London-based producer and vocalist Lauren Duffus and the great Bianca Scout. Jankowiak's last album, 2024's 'SHAME', laid down some of the groundwork, melting down '90s Polish hip-hop into endoskeleton for a cyberpunk fever dream, but 'Everything Always Changes' has a softer core and fixates on a far more romantic subject matter. 

Jankowiak's artistic inspiration for this one is a scene from 'Salto', a Kafkaesque Polish drama that peaks with a slow, dreamy dance. That's all you need to know, really; Jankowiak moves from here with real purpose, retaining that distinct rhythm and introducing his collaborators like dance partners moving across a haunted ballroom. Miller's turn on the title track neatly sets the scene, his gruff poetry stepping through the atmosphere  "Everything, always, changes," he annunciates slowly. Duffus and Scout sing in tandem on 'Stardust Garden', their voices just gently waltzing around Jankowiak's swooping strings and distorted, almost industrial pads. When Miller returns, his voice has been transformed into a cybernetic wail and Jankowiak resists the urge to meet it with rhythms, adding weightless gliding squares instead.

In fact, it takes until central track 'Salto' for the album's various threads to knot into more tangible shapes. Here, Duffus's voice is ushered to centre stage, propped up by booming kicks and rattly trills. "I'm haunted," she moans, displaying the same mystery and charisma that made last year's 'Can's Gone Warm' so crucial. Scout, meanwhile, gets her chance to shine on 'the quiet's song', singing a muted hymn over sparse Fairlight stabs and delicate piano flourishes. Thanks to Jankowiak's measured, directorial hand, the album never feels overwhelming, making for a record that's so much more than the sum of its considerable parts.

items.body:
One of the most distinctive and legendary vocal/dub albums of all time, recorded in 1981 by the “dub dentist” Keith Hudson, ‘Playing It Cool & Playing It Right’ is now back in circulation for the first time in over 20 years, when it was first given overdue flowers via Basic Channel And Honest Jon’s ‘Basic Replay’ programme. It still burns with a rare energy, making it an untouchable, foundational text for the ages.

Keith Hudson (1946-1984) was one of dub reggae’s most distinctive innovators, renowned for a run of classic solo albums and productions for U-Roy, Big Youth, Ken Boothe and Horace Andy between 1972 and his untimely passing in 1984. However, Hudson's late period is where the real imperial juice can be found, a time that saw him move from Jamaican to London and New York studios, applying his unfathomable production style to a heavily americanised strain of vocal Soul. ‘Playing It Cool & Playing It Right’ is the pinnacle of that late period, an album that builds layer upon layer of alchemical brilliance.

Hudson’s combination of hooks and complex, highly unusual production is really unlike anything else from the period, or since, crooning in a soul mode made more haunting by a discreetly judicious application of tape FX, endlessly heavy subs, and mixing desk tricks deployed to delirious, almost psycho-acoustic effect.  The album was originally meant to feature one of Hudson's teenage sons to voice the dubs, but in the event the Love Joys, Wayne Jarrett, and inimitably Hudson himself featured at the microphone, with the dozen cuts co-produced by Wackies founder Lloyd ‘Bullwackie’ Barnes - the only collaboration between the two producers. It was originally issued on Hudson’s own label, Joint International, with subsequent pressings on Basic Replay in 2003, making it increasingly sought-after in the years since. 

Alongside reggae’s first concept album, ‘Flesh of My Skin, Blood of My Blood’, ‘Playing It Cool’ remains one the genre’s most important and unusual releases, picking up new disciples with every new wave of listeners taken aback by its stark, brooding blooze and brittle, spectral rendering.

Returning to Shelter Press, INA GRM director François J. Bonnet collages harsh, feedback-dense textures, resonant chimes and disorienting synths, inking a serpentine narrative that's part Fennesz, part Valerio Tricoli, part Jake Muir.

There's a storyteller's flair to 'Sub Re', and that's not just because the title directly references Victor Hugo's 'Toilers of the Sea'. The veteran French sound artist fashions two sides of bumpy collaged plot points, drawing us in at first with dense electroacoustic guitar noise that wouldn't sound out of place on a loveliescrushing record. Referencing shoegaze merely in its full-on power, he cuts to Sonic Youth-style squealing feedback before submerging the cacophony completely, ducking it beneath smudged low-end rumbles and 'Mulholland Drive'-like hums. It sets the scene neatly for the next movement, where Bonnet introduces an ensemble of bells that slowly, surely gather momentum; imprinted with the rhythm of post-rock, believe it or not, it's a stretch that echoes Constellation's vital early releases, stirring tape noise and chimes with simple, pensive riffs that travel confidently from quiet to loud. 

But Bonnet never makes it that easy. Before long, these elements too have disappeared, replaced by subtly beating extended tones and xenharmonic wails that are skillfully merged with thick Sunn O)))-style drones, bringing us right back to where we started. And on the flip, Bonnet is just as ambitious, beginning with an industrial organ-scape that dissolves into an evocative hum of brassy notes and inclement field recordings. Even this feels like purposeful narrative red-herring because within moments, Bonnet brings the breathy pipe organ sounds bet, forming a light, major key crescendo that he uses to foreshadow the album's most drastic mood shift. The sun cracks through the rainclouds at last and we're lowered into a dry, verdant locale that's seemingly teeming with life. It's only in the last few minutes of the side when Bonnet seems to refer back to his last record, the impressionistic 'Shifted in Dreams', with a short blast of hypnagogic moodiness before the album flickers to a close.

The Sultans of Sludge slang a definitive label debut for Sub Pop, bringing their singular sound to roost on a legendary label local to their origins in the US north west, whose rugged landscapes fed directly into the LP’s formidably primal concentration of dualistic energies

Hailing some 30 years since Sunn O)))’s formation, their eponymous 10th studio album reckons with forces of nature - time and space, dark and light - for 80 minutes of air-shuddering pressure limning epic, craggy vistas from a thick haar of distortion. Subtly enlivened with field recordings made in forests near Bear Creek Studios, Woodinville, Washington, where O’Malley says they would “go hiking and be out in the woods, spend time outdoors”, the resulting six-part sequence sees the duo drill down to fundamentals with an absorbing sense of purpose and telepathically-attuned intuition. A notable dearth of other contributors also means it’s one of their truest statements as a duo; just Stephen O’Malley & Greg Anderson howling into the wilds on all instrumentation, from trusted axes to keys and electro-acoustic sorcery. 

At this point, not to labour the arboreal metaphors, but it may take a certified guide to see the wood for the trees in Sunn O))) lands, such is the uniquely coherent sprawl of their sound at 30 years up to the hilt in atonal rock doom. Our hair’s not long enough to lay claim as spirit guides, but after 23 years of bearing witness to them live, and ingesting most of their LPs, we can say this side is wholly emblematic of their radical steez. Between the two 18 minute totems of a ‘XXANN’ laced with location recording of running water at tender points, and a ‘Mindrolling’ monstered with claw-handed riffs, they take it to typically stare-down levels of intensity with the sustained threat of ‘Does Anyone Hear Like Venom?’, and billowing sheets of subharmonic distortion harnessed in ‘Everett Moses’. Closer ‘Glory Black’ is, however, a sort of sore thumb with a relatively conventional riff progression and rising banks of silvery wheeze that collapse into keys and field recordings, hearkening most closely to the duo’s precedents and NW peers in the Sub Pop roster, Earth, or even another touchstone, Black Sabbath, at their most strung out. 

Heavy as your life.

Gulp Joachim Nordwall’s queasiest, most curdled synth tones on this supremely detuned co-op with Athens’ Stellage crew = 45 minutes of pure nasal-drip tang and gungy pulses tipped FFO Connor Camburn, Wolf Eyes, Conrad Schnitzler, Ilpo Väisänen’s Liima alltimers.

Joachim Nordwall’s 1st solo jaunt since capping the ‘Healing Music’ series in ’23 finds the DIY linchpin and serial collaborator coaxing potently psychoactive tones from an undisclosed set up. It appears to be one of his most intently focussed jags in recent memory, concentrated on juicing a paucity of ingredients for optimal flavour. Nothing that new then? Well, aye, but when he really gets into it, with an effect that really probes parts of the psyche untouched by anything we’ve heard from him before, he produces synaesthetic sounds that frankly makes our ears salivate. 

A starting exercise in plucky pulse-work recalling Robert Aiki Aubrey Lowe initiates a real descent into the nether regions of Nordwall’s imagination, pulling into sepulchral drone on ‘Trance Recording’ and Droog wet dream material on ‘Abandoned Test Site’, while allowing for some levity in the lacquer-crackling pulse poem ‘Expand Your Mind’. However, he soon pitches back into resonant, metallic sonorities with durational conviction on a ‘Some Skies Overlap’ bringing to mind Connor Camburn works, but with an icier edge, and his title track spews molten drums in a rumbling, spark-spitting torrent. 

Proper filth. Snorkel it!

Pascual Martinez (young dude) and BPT head honcho Jeremy Castillo (unc) have spent the last few years in the stu, cooking up this deep fried, groovin' 4 tracker. Fans of 2011-16 LIES and Future Times releases, “Biology" era Young Marco, Juju and Jordash, and the Wah Wah Wino crew are in for a treat.

In an era where literally every aspect of dance music is overly programmed and manicured, ¿DONDEDOS take a massively refreshing approach marked by true experimentation. All drums were recorded on the Roland R8, and the melodies were live played with a loose, jammy feel not felt on many electronic 12" releases in 2026. They're a jam band baby!!!!! 

The fun starts with "Drifting Nowhere," a fried oddball deep house record with one of the year's most infectious basslines. Be ready for it to be on a loop in your brain long after the track has stopped playing.

2nd track "Dies Varos" was described by BPT fam Izaak from Loveshadow as sounding like "part of the Mediterranean touching Mexico." Ahhhhhhhhhhhhhhhhhhhhhh. (that was a deep relaxed sigh, not a scream for once!!!)

"Music for Patios" sounded pretty good on a walk and not on a patio so, just FYI, only a suggestion not a requirement. 

Ender Noche Caminando features Diego Herrera (AKA Suzanne Kraft) on sax. In Jeremy's own words, this track features "oddball dancehall drums on the R8 with 80s synth pop dub melodic sensibilities." "

Kev Martin inaugurates his LADYBUG singles series with a follow-up to 2020's 'In Blue', calling up Dis Fig to rebuild the first album's dread trip-hop "tunnel sound" concept from the ground up.

You can always rely on Felicia Chen to bring the pain and 'Vanishing' nestles confidently into the canon of leftfield break-up songs, led by a vocal that sounds like tears streaming down dusty, peeling wallpaper. Martin replies with typically spacious synths, swirling echoes and a rolling bassline that runs a line from Bristol to Kingston with dirty old twine. And aside from providing a dub, he builds an entirely new track - the ominous "Numb Mix" - dialing back the drums and pushing Chen's voice even further forward in the mix, accentuating its heartbreaking essence.

If you're into King Midas Sound or Adrian Sherwood, your time.

items.body:
Superb late night jazz-jungle fusion by recombinant specialist Antonio Marini’s cult unit, Healing Force Project, coolly nodding to Miles Davis via DJ Shadow, Pat Thomas and 4Hero or Peshay, in a signature, roving but holistic, richly visionary style

His first bow on Berlin’s Evighet label frames Marini deep in a mode of smouldering nocturnal substance that’s consistently snagged lugs since early turns for Acido, Berceuse Heroique and Firecracker identified them as one to keep a watch on in the early 2010s. In its shadow-strafing turns of low down Mo Wax beats, noirish dub touches and rudely loose but disciplined jungle ballistics it all feels like their most collected and thematically thorough work - dare we say even definitive - pursuing classic dragons with a playthru flow that’s a real pleasure to follow.

The eight tracks can’t help but remind us to being a young DJ Shadow fan in the late ‘90s/early ‘00s, and getting hard turned-off his music when reading him outright dismiss jungle/D&B in an interview. Across ‘Unholy Magnetic’, Healing Force Project almost imagines what Shadow could have sounded like if he embraced the ‘nuum, or took cues from Pat Thomas’ ‘New Jazz Jungle: Remembering’ (1997) at the time, as manifest in its eight cuts of deeply smoked out swerve and timeless verve. 

Louche spectres of prime era Mo Wax and ‘On the Corner’ Miles hang out on the slow, dubbed swanger ‘Where’s Doctor Who’, setting up a fleet-hooved suite prone to flash ruder fangs of jungle like Source Direct in spy jazz mode with ‘Cerebral Upload’, and peshay’s debonaire charms in ‘Cathode Rays’, while ‘The Groover’ tests out a sort of unchronic dubstep-jungle sound. But it’s most impressive in the way he tempers those bits with the downstrokes of simmered pressure in ‘The Ways of Golding Space & Flying’ hinting at 4 Hero’s ‘Parallel Universe’, or totally comes into his own on the drill-jungle fusion ‘Playing Tabla and Smoking Weed With Aliens’, thru the 11 mins of recursive dub to ‘Infinite (D[ub]rop.’

items.body:
Ezekiel Honig's glitchy, concréte house breakout, that originally surfaced nearly two decades ago, finally gets a new lease of life (and a fresh mastering job) thanks to the Keplar imprint.

Back in 2008, the world was already over microhouse. The glitchy, short-lived micro-genre had burned bright for a short moment; Philip Sherburne had coined the term in 2001 and by the time Akufen's 'My Way' had emerged just a year later it felt as if the shine had gone. Honig's 'Surfaces of a Broken Marching Band' arrived in 2008 and sounded like reformed traces of the recent past. The backbone was 4/4, crawling towards a slinky 120BPM minimal house, but the emotional content was completely different. This wasn't material that was aimed at the club or even the afterparty, it was loose, faded gear that Honig had made from meticulously collected foley sounds and environmental recordings - domestic elements that Matthew Herbert would be proud of.

And because the music slipped quietly into its own nook, it still sounds unique now, a record that deserves to be filed alongside Farben's early 12"s and Kit Clayton's iconic 'Nek Sanalet', even Ricardo Villalobos's primo gear - just peep the title track and tell us it doesn't sound like 'Easy Lee' made with a broken shortwave radio and a pinball table. Needless to say, if you're into Mark Templeton (who incidentally appears twice on this record) or the soon-to-be-hauntological Y2K aesthetic, you'll need to grab it without delay.

items.body:
Paean to Wilson was arguably Vini Reilly and The Durutti Columns most important piece of work since the demise of the original Factory Records in the early 1990’s.

Reissued in close proximity to Paul Morley’s biography of the pivotal Manchester impressario and co-founder of Factory Records, ‘A Paean To Wilson’ expresses Vini’s enduring admiration for the man who gave him his first record deal, and continued to sing his praises until he passed in 2007.

The feeling is clearly mutual as the record unfolds as one of Vini’s most tender works since his Factory era, transmuting love and respect into 18 lyrical instrumentals and a few songs featuring vox, including canny use of Tony’s sardonic query “is this an artform, or are you just a technician” that trails off into vaporous contrails on the gorgeous, 10 minute long ‘Chant’ - perhaps the finest Durutti in years.

"The Durutti Column was Tony Wilson's baby. We were the first act signed up to his Factory club night and the first band signed to Factory Records. Over the years we worked on many albums together and the one thing that Tony and I always argued about was that he thought that I should make music and write rather than sing.

After he died, I decided to make a body of work which did not have traditional song structures and which was concerned solely with the musical content. My only objective was to create some music that Tony would thoroughly approve of. I think I've done that and, if his spirit lives on - which I like to think think it does - I want him to know that this is for him." 

Vini Reilly

items.body:
Oren Ambarchi's kraut-techno-free jazz magnum opus is back for its 10th anniversary -  an ambitious ensemble piece featuring an all-star list of players including Ricardo Villalobos, Keith Fullerton Whitman, Mark Fell, crys Cole, Will Guthrie, Arto Lindsay and Konrad Sprenger... Wooooo

You've got to admire Ambarchi's chutzpah here. 'Hubris' is an all you can eat buffet of his various musical cravings, a chance for his friends, influences and collaborators to flex a little and for Ambarchi to attempt to ride the groove like an experienced cowboy on an out-of-control bucking bronco. The first side is the biggest surprise, a dedication to Wang Chung's enduring, disco-influenced 'To Live and Die in L.A.' soundtrack that begins with ping-ponging guitar notes and Jim O'Rourke's synth blips, before elusive Berlin-based composer Konrad Sprenger (aka Joerg Hiller) drops in with some motorized guitar vamps. It's rhythmic gear that fits in with the Berlin school until Mark Fell appears in the final third with some typically fractured percussion.

On the flip, the groove loosens after a short guitar interlude. Ricardo Villalobos takes over with a suitably winding, minimal throb over live rhythms played by Joe Talia and Will Guthrie simultaneously as krautrock techno mutates into disco fusion. Keith Fullerton Whitman tries to nudge the track off the rails with his modular expositions, but the path is set - Arto Lindsay's axe is just the icing on the cake. By the end of the side, we're in full jazz-noise mode: everything's still pegged to Villalobos' central pulse, but that's the only element that's bolted down. 

Hard to believe it's 10 years already - we can't think of a better skeleton key to unlock the secrets behind Black Truffle's musical identity.

items.body:
Memotone’s sublime, world-building ambient-jazz-fusion project yields a total gem for Accidental Meetings, perfused with the presence of Ugné Uma, Typesun & Jabu on a new highlight of his personalised microcosm, tipped for anyone on the line from Savath & Savalas to Moritz Von Oswald Trio, The Necks to Laurel Halo.

Active since 2011, it’s been a real pleasure to hear Will Yates cultivate his memotone sound into something more complex, yet not necessarily more complicated, on a slew of LPs for the likes of TTT, Sähkö, and World of Echo, plus that ace cut on Carrier’s debut LP. Club music is now long in the rearview, while ambient and jazz musics have taken precedence as the multi-instrumentalist continues to diversify his creative binds across more free-formed, expressive soundscapes, breezing with elements of spiritual jazz as much as psych folk, post rock,contemporary classical and strands of electronic music. 

‘Warm Shadows’ features some of his most seductive and expansive work, shaped with an underlying grasp of abstract, instrumental narratives that have become his calling card during this last decade. Intimacy and slowness are key to his exquisitely hushed appeal; unfolding the softest brushstrokes with patient electroacoustic nuance and attention to detail on two standouts with emergent Lithuanian vocalist Ugné Uma, who channels a mix of smouldering spiritual jazz and Eastern European melancholy on ‘Laimèti Pavyksta’, and even Sade-esque soul on the dusky closer ‘You Are Different.’ 

Elsewhere, the Bristolian connection makes for another highlight with Jabu’s Jasmine Butt’s subtle contribution to ‘Round The Bend,’ comparable to something from BoC’s ‘Campfire Headphase’, but left to his own devices memotone proves a consummate, atmospheric storyteller. Opener ‘For The Feral’ feels like a miniature of The Necks, and his feel for dreamy electro-acoustic texture best comes into play on ‘One Winged Bird’ and the tongue-tip moisture in the air of ‘The Freedom,’ all pointing to an artist arguably in their imperial phase. 

Tip!

items.body:
A digestibly pared-down version of Félicia Atkinson's 90-minute score to Georges Franju's controversial French horror film 'Les yeux sans visage' ('Eyes Without A Face'), 'SANS VISAGE' is her most sinister material to date, made on piano and keyboards and improvised to the film. 

Atkinson was just a teenager when she first saw Franju's 1960 film and it moved her enough that when she was approached by Belgian cultural institute VIERNULVIER to work on a new score, she knew exactly how to approach it. She remembered how impactful the film's themes had been and how resonant they were even decades later, where violence against women is still nauseatingly commonplace. In the film, an adaptation of an even more disturbing novel by Jean Redon, a plastic surgeon stalks and kills women who look like his disfigured daughter, removing their faces in an attempt to create a new one for her. Atkinson dedicates her slow-motion, menacing soundtrack to Gisèle Pelicot, remarking how patriarchal violence cycles again and again through history, creating cages within cages for women. But there's hope; Atkinson doesn't languish in darkness and terror, she knows that in there somewhere, liberation might be on the horizon. 

Underneath the grim, gloomy electric piano notes and agonising pauses, Atkinson seems to relish in a sense that escape might be possible. And if you've seen the film then you'll realise that she's acknowledging the fact that Dr. Génessier, the antagonistic surgeon, meets a fittingly grisly end. While he's let off the hook by police, his daughter Christiane is horrified by his crimes, freeing the dogs he was experimenting on and letting them take their revenge. It's a horror film, after all. But Aktinson swerves all the usual tropes; she improvises an impressionistic dream of wailing tones and aborted phrases that centre the resolution, not the torture itself. Re-scores are often a creative dead end, but thankfully this one adds texture, color and new context to the source material - it makes us want to watch the film all over again.

Barcelona-based Argentine sound artist Dima uses mythology to re-examine her personal world on 'Salva', dissolving instrumental phrases with confounding granular processes and allowing fragile trip-hop-inspired songs to emerge from the ambiance.

There's an unexpected balance on 'Salva'. At first, on the opener 'SOELAR' or its breathy follow-up 'APOGEO', you might think you have it figured out, its atmospheric blend of plasticky flutes and sci-fi pads. But as the latter track hits its third act, something unexpected appears - Dima's voice was already there, haunting the soundscape, but when a slowed-down beat joins it provides a real surprise. And 'Salva' keeps rocking from side to side, never settling into a reliable groove. On 'QUANTUM', Dima sings into an echoing void almost unaccompanied, but on 'FOLDING INWARD', she adds atmospheric synths and gong-y resonances to go in another direction, moving away from song structure towards grim abstraction. 

And after the one-two punch of the album's poppiest tracks, 'REACH' and 'IT HAD TO BURN', Dima concludes with 'Inked', a throbbing dark ambient nightmare that seems to dive deep beneath an alien ocean. Terrifying stuff.

items.body:
New LP from French-born, London-based composer and musician Pascal Bideau via Tonal Union.

"Cartographers and US multinational technology corporations might think they’ve mapped out most of our big, beautiful blue planet, and yet there’s always more to discover if you know where to look. French-born, London-based composer and musician Pascal Bideau takes this as his central premise on a new album of intrepid sonic exploration that delights in the sensation of being somewhere you’ve never been before. ‘Terra Incognita’ invites us to seven faraway sonic imaginariums fusing global and spiritual jazz with life affirming minimalism into a hypnotic, polyrhythmic odyssey.

This time, the albums’ sound palette is more vibrant, earthy and abundant, drawing inspiration from the radiating optimism and high-energy sources heard in Afrobeat, Highlife and Electronic Afro-pop music, sounding looser, free and primarily interested in raw sensations. Antithetical to the precise ostinatos and gamelan patterns of the acclaimed debut ‘Fleeting Future’ (2022) and ‘Lines’ (2023). Terra Incognita, then, is a hybrid blend of traditional music and modern electronics, a trip into the unknown that ambulates freely, taking pleasure in its repetitions and never staying still. Bideau suggests this unmarked territory could be as much a fantasyland as it is a transportive journey into the inner self."

items.body:
Working his hi-BPM (bull)rushes into swampy environmental recordings, Richie Culver returns to Boro's Industrial Coast with his most impressionistic and substantial Quiet Husband set so far, short-circuiting distinctions between his visual and aural practices with keenly synaesthetic nous hugely advised to admirers of W92’s Omen Wapta, aspects of Chain Reaction’s Matrix, or even H-Fusion’s ‘Captured Entities’.

‘The Architecture of Perception’ examines the lived and structural correspondences between techno and painting, proposing that tracks in the club function as colours do in the studio. On 'Composition', Culver sketches out his rough blueprint; first playing rich, noisy nighttime sounds - chirping crickets, oozing liquids - before looping them behind knee-trembling 185BPM kicks and metallic clangs. It's music that seems to revel in its own contradictory nature: minimal maximalism; faster, grubbier and more provocative than you'd ever expect to hear in a club.

'Abstraction' dispenses with the rhythm altogether, concentrating on creeping and evocative jungle ambiance that lubricates the brain for 'Duration’, where Culver's concept snaps into gear with buzzing cybernetic calls and sonorous outdoor sounds that dissolve into undulating 4/4 thuds. It'd be daft to label it dub techno, but if you compare Culver's muckiest gear to Basic Channel's earliest, most saturated mixing desk experiments, there's a similar level of intentionality: an understanding of space and tonal colour that permeates the rippling drive of the music. And Culver never lets his breakneck dancefloor instincts take precedence over his blustery experiments. The momentum flips back and forth, darting from the dancefloor to the bathrooms to the darkroom, heading outside for a lungful of fresh air (or a cig) before taking an about turn and rummaging thru it all again.

TENGGER releases self-titled 13th album via We Are Busy Bodies.

"The blissed family band is back! TENGGER have always moved together, through time, space & genre. 'SKY' arrives as a new chapter: a little more still, a little more inward, while keeping all the warmth that's always been at the heart of what they do.

Embodying the band name meaning "endless sky" in Mongolian and "vast sea" in Hungarian, their 8th album 'SKY' centres on the feelings of boundless, infinite expansion. Conceived as one continuous environment rather than a collection of tracks, the album unfolds slowly through luminous synths, patient drones and Itta's breath-like vocals. 

Like a soft big sky you can actually float on: 'SKY' is vast, warm, and wide open.

"Rather than a specific emotion, we hope the record opens a certain awareness — that the sky is not just something to be seen. Through it, we sense a connection to something much larger — a feeling of being linked to the wider universe. This sense of connection runs through the entire record." "

Bristol’s leading bassbin drivers indulge their passion for a spectrum of speedy UKG to US ghettotech style & pattern at 140-150BPM as BAGS INC.

"Bristol's Sam Binga & Addison Groove have been friends and collaborators since their 2013 'BS3' EP, released on Modeselektor's '50 Weapons' imprint. This project, the third full-length on Binga’s Pineapple Records, is born from an intense 72-hour session at the legendary Devon Analogue Studios, where the pair were able to explore their mutual love of uptempo machine funk - whether that be Detroit Jit, Chicago Boxjams or Turbo Electro.

Three days of intense creativity across classic drum machines, vintage analogue synths and rare hardware effects resulted in a collection of raw but powerful audio building blocks - and over the past two years, the pair have been gradually shaping them into what is now a complete project - the BAGS INC album. Across 12 tracks, Binga & Addison explore that exciting space between 140 and 150 bpm - but while it's fast, it's not 'hard'; as you'd expect from the creators, it's still got that wiggle, and the all-important cheekiness for which they're known."

Heavy-lidded, late nite jazz-soul suss from the keenly touted Ugné Uma & producer emer, secreting a dozen sleepwalker specials on their duo debut with Stroom. FFO Leila, Lolina, ML Buch, Tirzah, Voice Actor.

Hashed out in imaginary air between Brussels and Berlin, ‘You and Me’ projects a mutual dream sequence of downbeat stardust and midnight jazz vapours supposed by two emergent figures of the EU undergrowth: one Ugné Uma paying up on the promise of her single for Somewhere Press, plus Marija Rasa’s emer, still fresh from a standout solo debut LP on Short Span in late ’25. In duo, they reaffirm, double down, and transcend the sum of their parts with a classy grasp of sandman tekkerz, suspending bodies between duvet-dive beatdown and hypnagogic soul with a slow-burn frisson of romantic intimacy.

With no hard edges or surprises for the supine mind, the album unfolds in its own liminal space with a gauzy sense of daydreamy-into-nocturnal physics. The filigree dub of emer’s ‘Fog’ LP is found dialled down to more powdery ambient jazz and soul smoulder, and inflected with a fine-wrought R&B discipline that ideally swirls Uma’s classic, smoky delivery, to the natural extent that it feels like they’ve been cooking together for years. Dusted but not dusty, it all treads the finest line of classic and modernist late nite needs for the ages, and especially hot, sleepless hours.

Reissue of the debut by A.G. Cook & Danny L Harle’s earliest duo, Dux Content, initially dispensed on Gamsonite, a predecessor of P.C. Music, and teasing out strands of makina, electro-house, bardcore and trap with combo’s of ludic, recombinant suss & sharp sound design that became their calling card.

Scrolling back to what now feels like a distant world - the up-for-grabs edges of early 2010s - ‘Lifestyle’ maps out formative aspects of the two producers, still relatively fresh from music studies at Goldsmiths, and making their mark in a burgeoning “internet music” scene. Of course they’re both now chart-topping songwriters/producers with credits for Charli xcx, Dua Lipa, Oklou, et al, but here they’re positively bubbling over with wild, yet disciplined, fusions of upfront hard dance with jazz, contemporary classical and pop that, with the benefit of hindsight, place them in a contemporaneous cultural slipstream with likes of Cracksmurf/T C F or James Ferraro, and soon-to-be spar, SOPHIE.

‘Lifestyle’ is the sound of two minds scything thru cultures and sounds they grew up with - Harle coming from a family background spanning his Geordie dad, John Harle’s BBC scores and early taste for makina’s stacked melodies - and bonding over a shared love of Captain Beefheart, Archie Sheep, and Tim & Eric, all evident in their grasp of shiny, commercial hooks and complex rhythm wrapped up with daft grin and wink. Shake a wand anywhere and you’ll hit a mad one, from the crazed midi piano house of ‘Voice of an Angel’, thru the jazz-fink of ‘City Break’ and ‘Hero Next Door’, free wheeling jazz trance of ‘Heart of Death’ and pitch bent panpipes of ‘Business Class’.

items.body:
Finally, Kompakt issue a true GAS outlier on vinyl for the first time, recorded in 1989 and containing some of Wolfgang Voigt’s earliest and starkest recycling of magisterial Wagner loops, closest to the ends of The Caretaker, Philip Jeck, Kevin Drumm.

One of those releases that has lurked on our shelves since 2008 as a book and CD, ‘November 89’ exists in the margins of Wolfgang Voigt’s GAS canon as its creepiest and most occluded evocation of long walks in the Bavarian forests. While other GAS classics ooze a sort of dappled warmth breaking thru the trees in their widescreen dub techno strolls, you can fully feel the light dying over the horizon and the forest drawing in on this particularly gloomy, hour-long suite. 

As the title suggests, it was mostly, remarkably, made in ’89, back when Voigt was finding his feet between techno, house and indie-pop, and nearly a decade before he co-founded Kompakt with Michael Mayer & Jürgen Paape - by which time he was a full-fledged rave dynamo as Love Inc. and myriad others notable projects. And, in that sense, it can be heard as his ‘Selected Ambient Works 89-95’ - or perhaps more pertinently with SAW II vibes - in his nascent attempt to chase the ambient dragon, which surely endures for its strangely nostalgic, unheimlich qualities.

An educated guess leads us to think the first three were made in ’89, taking in the nightfall scenery of smudged symphonic strings and icy crackle to ‘Der Wald’, plus the muddied bass waltz and spectral pall of ‘Das Moor’, thru the self-evidently titled centrepiece ‘1989-11-01’, bristling with a digitally iridescent dread. ‘Tal 90’ and ‘Nah Und Fern’, which shares its title with the 2008 boxset, were most likely made a little later, and find the wintry doom thawing to the GAS-eous forms we’ve all come to deeply know and adore. 

A true evergreen for deep ambient techno connoisseurs, no less

items.body:
An advanced masterclass in Berlin beat science, ‘Wireless’ is the final and arguably strongest solo release by T++; aka Torsten Pröfrock, an artist with a long lineage of important releases under numrous aliases - Dynamo, Erosion,Log, Resilent, Traktor, Various Artists and more - a true pillar of Berlin's Techno legacy.

First issued by Honest Jon’s in 2010, the 2x12” features samples of singer and ndingidi-player Ssekinomu (originally found on the EMI archival dive ‘Bellyachers, Listen - Songs From East Africa, 1938-46’) reworked by Pröfrock into a volley of rambunctious but rudely disciplined club workouts some 75 years later. In many other hands, this could have been just another passable cut ’n splice edit, but T++ treats the material with a balance of reverence and raving license, highlighting an instinctive understanding of the original music's intent and purpose, and their deep rooted connection to modern fast rap and hardcore dance musics.

The four tracks amount to a contemporary classic in their field and also exist in a strong tradition of German artists ranging from Stockhausen to Can and Basic Channel whose music has crucially incorporated the fluid, rolling nature and spectra of African drumming patterns. However, it’s vital to point out that T++’s take on African drumming is also filtered thru a love of UK music - Jungle, D&B, garage, dubstep - meaning that his rhythms are properly underlined with syncopated, technoid basslines owing as much to Kingston, Jamaica as Brixton and Sheffield in the UK.

For anyone who had been intently listening to Pröfrock's output since his Traktor gems, thru his Dynamo aces, to early work with Monolake and his string of seminal T++ 12”s in the 2000’s, on its release in 2010 ‘Wireless’ quickly came to epitomise his approach to broken techno production at its most open-ended and inexorable. Between the itchy, sprung step of ‘Cropped’, the puckish darkside torque of ‘Anyi’, a voodoo communal in ‘Voice No Bodies’, and the reanimated spirits of ‘Dig’ you have some of the finest mutant techno ever cut to vinyl.

An absolute must-have for dancers and DJs.

items.body:
Remastered and returned to vinyl for the first time since 1959, 'Blues in the Mississippi Night' is one of Alan Lomax's most impactful recordings, a historical document of the blues and the Black culture that surrounds it that was so controversial at the time it had to be released under pseudonyms. This new edition arrives with full transcriptions and detailed liner notes.

In 1947, just a few years before he escaped to London during the McCarthy era, Lomax invited legendary bluesmen Big Bill Broonzy, Memphis Slim and Sonny Boy Williamson to perform at the Town Hall in New York City as part of his Midnight Special concert series. He shuttled them over to the nearby Decca Studios and warmed up the machines, asking them not just to perform some of their well-known standards, but to discuss "the blues" - the legacy of the music itself and the realities of Black life in America, warts and all. It's hard to relay just how controversial this was at the time; Black folks knew, but to white America it was an elaborate fiction, a grim Jim Crow-era reality they weren't ready to accept. And when the stories were printed in the Common Ground magazine under the title 'I Got the Blues', they caused so much outcry that the album's release was delayed for a decade. In the interim period, Lomax used snippets of the session for the BBC Radio documentary 'The Art of the Negro. And even when it was eventually pressed by United Artists in 1959, it was attributed to "Natchez, Sib & Leroy", made-up names that protected the identities of the artists themselves, in case of repercussions. 

Listening back now, it's enlightening, putting an often misunderstood American reality into sharp focus. The album is hinged on conversations between two of the artists: Broonzy, an ex-sharecropper who had served in the First World War before picking up guitar on the Chicago circuit and Slim, a bandleader and long-time associate of Broonzy's whose distinctive piano playing defined the era. Proper blues standards, prison songs and chants are woven instinctively into the conversation to contextualize the words and it's incredibly effective; the culture itself should already be telling us the story, but it's even more tangible when we hear the words from two old friends recounting their lived reality. And it's far more valuable to hear this - a primary source - than the rantings of ornery collectors and critics.

items.body:
In spring 2025, Abul Mogard and Rafael Anton Irisarri created the source material for their second album, Where Light Pauses in the Silence of the Sun, during a three-day residency at Morphine Raum in Berlin.

"Functioning as both recording studio and performance venue, the space has no stage, with the audience gathered around the performers. Working within an open framework, the duo reshaped the music each evening while recording the performances live to multitrack. Rotary speakers, modular synthesizers and bowed guitar formed the core of their sonic language, captured through a 1970s mixing console and microphones placed around the room.

Back in Mogard’s studio in Rome, the material was further crafted as motifs were stretched, fragments isolated, and tempos dissolved. Irisarri recorded additional guitar textures and treatments in New York, while passages recorded by Martina Bertoni and Andrea Burelli in Berlin reinforced the harmonic centres and brought breath, refinement and a new sensibility to their compositions. The process continued as Mogard’s layering and subtraction reassembled everyone’s parts into the final arrangement.

The album opens with “In the Eastern Wild,” building from a sparse outline into a monumental formation of low-frequency weight, its internal motion shaped by the rotating Leslie speaker. “Over the Domes” widens into a broader acoustic field, where sustained modular tones meet waves of softly plucked guitar. The music then turns inward with “A Blue Descent,” centred on Bertoni’s cello, whose growling timbre introduces a melancholic depth.

At the album’s centre, “In a Quiet Radiance” unfolds around a slow guitar ostinato, its luminous stillness opening into a more expansive and reflective state. Across its ten-minute span, Burelli’s violin lines and Bertoni’s lower cello phrases gradually surface, weaving through the harmonic field. Mogard brings Burelli’s processed voice to the fore, its emotive, operatic presence becoming one of the record’s pivotal moments. “Of Blessed Ages” suspends the sonic flow, shifting between parallel major and minor chords as lingering, slowly decaying melodies shape the music’s internal drift. The closing “Among Shadows” settles into a darker resonance as layered textures recede.

Mogard and Irisarri’s shared language balances restraint and maximalism. UK magazine Crack describes the music as “a tidal wave held in suspension,” while Dutch newspaper de Volkskrant writes, “What a colossal sound, and how this music strikes at the emotions.” Reflecting on the residency sessions, Irisarri recalls: “At moments I genuinely couldn’t tell if a sound was coming from me or from Abul. It stopped feeling like two people making decisions and began to feel like we were inside a system moving on its own."

Marja de Sanctis’ cover artwork revisits the vessel sculpture from the duo’s first album, Impossibly Distant, Impossibly Close. There it appeared as raw, unfired clay. Here it has been fired in the kiln and finished with a glaze. Light gathers on its polished surface and spills into the surrounding space. As she explains, “I wanted to convey the idea of continuity within the duo, and the vessel became a kind of container for that idea. However, their music felt different this time, and with the collaboration of Martina and Andrea, I felt it should have a sleeker, softer, more glamorous look, very distant from the first raw appearance.” The transformation of the vessel from raw clay to fired form suggests a passage from immediacy toward permanence, mirroring the music’s gradual expansion."

Sandwell District’s Dave Sumner aka Function completes his Existenz cycle for Tresor with an expansive, full spectrum strafe from beat-less ambient to slow acid, electro and signature deep techno gems.

Seven years since his ‘Existenz’ album for Tresor, and leading on from related EPs for Rrose’s Eaux and his own Infrastructure New York, Sumner reflects on what prompted his LP, and interim strife, across six tracks tallying to an LP in their own right. After immersion in his patented style of nocturnal pads and lustrous acid lines, it shouldn’t be hard to identify his touch on some of Sandwell District’s most romantic high points, finely-sculpted in a style that has served him damn well since the mid-late ‘90s origins of NYC & Brum techno.

Shine-eyed reflections of early ‘90s electronica radiate from opener ‘Ascent’ into 12 mins of sleekly heady, decelerated acid house less on ‘City of Luz’, and what could almost be an SD cut in the mouth-watering detailing and elegant drive of ‘Transmutation’. He continues to hanker for lushness in the club on the whirring, melancholic offbeat propulsion to another standout, ‘Growth Cycle (Hermetic Mix)’, before turning darker with flashes of Kraftwerk-via-his NYC electro touchstones on ‘November 29’, and deferred gratification of ‘Rubedo’.
